techniques.name: Monotonicity Constraints
techniques.description: Monotonicity constraints require a model's prediction to move only one way as a chosen input rises, with the other inputs held fixed, so that, for example, predicted salary never falls as years of experience increase. The direction for each constrained feature is set from domain knowledge before training, and the learning algorithm or model structure then rules out any fit that breaks it, so the model cannot learn reversals that come from noise or sampling quirks in the data. Boosted-tree libraries apply the constraint when they choose splits and monotonic neural networks build it into their structure, while penalty-based methods only discourage violations. Because a penalty, a constraint set on the wrong column or a later processing step can still let a reversal through, testers then vary each constrained input across its range over many generated or real cases, with the other inputs fixed, and count any prediction that moves the wrong way. The evidence is that violation count, expected to be zero, together with a comparison of held-out accuracy with and without the constraint.

example_use_cases.description: A mortgage lender constrains its approval model so that higher income, longer employment and a higher credit score can only raise the approval score. Loan officers can then tell an applicant that improving any of these factors can only help the application, and the lender can state each factor's direction to its regulator.

A water utility's pipe-burst risk model is constrained so that risk rises with pipe age and operating pressure and falls with the quality of recent maintenance. Asset managers can then explain the ranked inspection list to the regulator through three directional rules, instead of an opaque score.

A hospital analytics team builds a tree-based model that predicts the cost of care for each patient and constrains the prediction never to fall as age or number of chronic conditions rises. Before release they sweep each constrained feature across its range for thousands of generated patient records, with the other features held fixed, and confirm that no prediction moves the wrong way. They also compare held-out accuracy with and without the constraints.

A utility's day-ahead demand forecast for office buildings is constrained so that predicted demand never falls as occupancy or floor area rises. The validation team writes this as an automated test that draws random building profiles, raises one constrained input at a time and fails the build if any forecast drops, so a retrained model that breaks the rule is caught before deployment.

limitations.description: Forces a one-way relationship even where the real one reverses, such as an inverted U between experience and performance. The model then fits that feature worse and cannot show the turning point, so held-out accuracy should be compared with and without the constraint.

Choosing which features to constrain, and in which direction, needs domain expertise. A wrong constraint builds a false belief into the model, and the check on the trained model will still pass, because it shows only that the constraint holds, not that it is right.

The rule covers one feature with the others held fixed, and says nothing about the size of the effect. A model can meet it by ignoring the feature, and when correlated inputs move together a person's overall score can still fall as one favourable input rises, so the constraint does not make the whole model easy to explain.

Support differs by model family. Tree-boosting libraries such as XGBoost accept constraints directly, while neural networks need a special architecture or a penalty term. With histogram-based tree methods, constraints can remove every candidate split and leave shallow trees that underfit.

A sweep or property-based test samples the input space. It can find a violation but cannot prove there is none, and a pass depends on how well the generated inputs cover realistic and rare combinations of features.

A straightforward method for implementing and  training  a  monotonic  network  is  described. We  apply  monotonic  networks  to  a  real-world  task  in  corporate  bond  rating  prediction  and  compare  them to other approaches.

resources.title: Application of the Back Propagation Neural Network Algorithm with Monotonicity Constraints for Two‐Group Classification Problems*
resources.abstract: Neural network techniques are widely used in solving pattern recognition or classification problems. However, when statistical data are used in supervised training of a neural network employing the back‐propagation least mean square algorithm, the behavior of the classification boundary during training is often unpredictable. This research suggests the application of monotonicity constraints to the back propagation learning algorithm. When the training sample set is preprocessed by a linear classification function, neural network performance and efficiency can be improved in classification applications where the feature vector is related monotonically to the pattern vector. Since most classification problems in business possess monotonic properties, this technique is useful in those problems where any assumptions about the properties of the data are inappropriate.

resources.title: An informed monotone neural network for multi-stage chronic kidney disease prediction with integrated GFR estimation
resources.abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a progressive condition affecting over 850 million people worldwide, where timely detection and accurate staging are critical to reducing morbidity, mortality, and healthcare burden. Current machine learning approaches often treat CKD prediction as a binary task, neglecting the ordered nature of disease stages, and rarely incorporate physiological constraints or calibrated probability estimates essential for clinical decision support. We propose a multi-stage CKD prediction framework that integrates ordinal classification, probability calibration, and a serum creatinine-monotonicity constraint within a knowledge distillation paradigm. A calibrated CatBoost model serves as a teacher, transferring temperature-scaled class probabilities to an ordinal neural network student augmented with an auxiliary eGFR regression task. Evaluated on a cohort of 750 patients from Al-Ramadi Teaching Hospital, our approach achieved superior macro-F1 and reduced expected calibration error. This work demonstrates that combining ordinal learning, calibration, and physiological constraints yields models that are not only accurate but also aligned with clinical reasoning, offering a pathway toward safer and more trustworthy AI tools for CKD management. Limitations like circular reasoning and target leakage are also discussed.

sample_claims.text: Every constrained input in the mortgage model has a documented direction of effect, so loan officers can tell an applicant that, other details being equal, higher income never lowers the approval score.
The clinical risk score is documented as never falling when a vital-sign measure worsens, other measures being equal, and clinicians are given that rule before they use the score.
In property-based testing over generated patient records, raising age or the number of chronic conditions on its own never lowered the cost model's prediction, and the test is rerun on every release
In sweeps of each constrained input across its full range, the building demand forecast recorded no case where predicted demand fell as occupancy rose.
Across 100,000 generated applicant records, raising income alone never lowered the lending model's predicted approval probability.
